parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A loudspeaker drives air in a tube open at the left and closed by a piston at the right. The displacement pattern is shown. The sound frequency stays constant as the piston moves left until the next shorter resonant length is reached. What are the initial and final harmonics?

A. First then first
B. First then second
C. Third then first
D. Third then second

answer.text: C. The initial pattern has three quarter-wavelength sections, so it is the third harmonic. The next shorter allowed pattern has one quarter-wavelength section: the first harmonic.

The first harmonic in a pipe with one open and one closed end has wavelength 60 cm. Which other wavelength can form a standing wave in this pipe?

A. 10 cm
B. 15 cm
C. 20 cm
D. 45 cm

answer.text: C. The allowed harmonics are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency, with wavelengths λ₁/n for odd n. For n=3, λ=60/3=20 cm.

parts.display_text: A standing wave forms in a pipe open at one end and closed at the other. Its length is L and sound speed is V. For positive integer n, which expression gives its harmonics? A. (2n−1)V/(2L)  B. (2n−1)V/(4L)  C. nV/(2L)  D. nV/(4L)

answer.text: Official answer B; editorial worked explanation: A closed-open pipe has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Its allowed wavelengths satisfy L = (2n−1)λ/4, so f_n = V/λ = (2n−1)V/(4L).
answer.evidence: Official May 2023 Physics HL Paper 1 TZ1 answer grid checked on PDF page 3; explanation independently calculated from the visible source question.

parts.display_text: The source diagram shows the standing wave on a fixed-length string driven at 120 Hz. Draw the standing wave observed on the same string when the oscillator frequency is 180 Hz.

answer.text: Official markscheme construction; editorial worked explanation: The 120 Hz pattern contains two half-wavelength loops. For the same string and wave speed, harmonic frequency is proportional to the number of half-wavelengths. Since 180/120=3/2, the new pattern must contain three half-wavelength loops between the same endpoints, with nodes at each end and two equally spaced internal nodes.

parts.display_text: A 210 Hz loudspeaker drives sound in a 1.20 m pipe with one closed end and one open end. The source diagram shows the established standing wave. Outline how the standing wave is formed in the pipe.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The sound wave travels down the pipe and reflects at the closed end. The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions. Their superposition produces the standing-wave pattern.

answer.text:

The displayed mode contains three quarter-wavelength sections, so L = 3λ/4. Hence λ = 4L/3 = 4(1.20)/3 = 1.60 m.

parts.display_text: The source diagram shows a 210 Hz standing wave in a 1.20 m pipe with one closed end and one open end. The frequency is reduced to 140 Hz. Explain why a standing wave will not form.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The shown 210 Hz mode is the third harmonic, so the first-harmonic frequency is 210/3 = 70 Hz. A one-open/one-closed pipe supports only odd multiples of this frequency: 70, 210, 350 Hz, and so on. Since 140 Hz is an even multiple, it cannot satisfy the closed-end node and open-end antinode conditions.

parts.display_text:
Two opposite travelling sound waves form a standing wave. Which statement defines a displacement antinode?

A. A position whose displacement is always at its maximum value
B. A position whose particles never move
C. A position of maximum oscillation amplitude
D. A position of minimum oscillation amplitude

answer.text: C. At a displacement antinode, particles oscillate with the greatest amplitude. Their instantaneous displacement still passes through zero each cycle.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An oscillator initially has displacement +1.2 cm and is at rest. Its original undamped period is T. It is immersed in thick oil and subsequently experiences heavy damping.

(a) Explain damping in terms of forces and energy.
(b) Sketch a possible displacement–time graph from 0 to 2T, showing the return towards equilibrium.

answer.text:
(a) A resistive force removes energy from the oscillator and transfers it to the surroundings.
(b) Start at x = +1.2 cm with zero initial slope. The displacement decreases towards zero without crossing it or oscillating. After the initial response, the curve progressively flattens as it approaches equilibrium; it need not reach zero by 2T.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A ship has natural heave frequency 0.13 Hz. The wave encounter frequency would be 0.120 Hz if the ship stopped and 0.0525 Hz if it continued moving. Explain what resonance means and deduce which option keeps the ship steadier.

answer.text:
Editorial worked explanation, checked against the official mark scheme:

Resonance occurs when driving frequency equals natural frequency and amplitude is maximal. Using the supplied encounter frequencies, 0.120 Hz when stopped is close to the 0.13 Hz natural frequency, while 0.0525 Hz when moving is much farther away. Continuing to move therefore keeps the ship steadier.

An open-open tube contains a standing sound wave with three nodes. How many antinodes does it have?

A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 4

answer.text:
Official key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. Each open end is a displacement antinode. Nodes and antinodes alternate, so three internal nodes require four antinodes: one at each end and two between the nodes.

A tube has a mouthpiece node at one end and an open-end antinode at the other. Its first harmonic is 92 Hz. Which sequence can the tube produce?

A. 92,138,184,230 Hz
B. 92,184,276,368 Hz
C. 92,276,460,644 Hz
D. 92,276,828,1288 Hz

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two equal waves form a standing wave with three nodes and two antinodes on a fixed string. Their frequency is doubled. How many antinodes are in the new standing wave?

A. 1  B. 2  C. 3  D. 4

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. Two antinodes correspond to the second harmonic of the fixed string. With wave speed and string length unchanged, doubling frequency halves wavelength and doubles the harmonic number from 2 to 4. The new pattern therefore has four antinodes.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A violin string is fixed at both ends. (a) Explain how a standing wave forms when it is plucked. (b) Its first-harmonic pattern is supplied. The tension is 71.5 N, length 0.32 m and mass per unit length 2.03×10⁻³ kg m⁻¹. Frequencies for strings 1–4 are 196, 294, 440 and 659 Hz. Identify the string. (c) Compare the standing wave on the string with the travelling sound wave in air.

answer.text: Official markscheme result: string 2, with f≈293 Hz. Editorial worked explanation: A travelling disturbance reflects at the fixed peg and bridge. Incident and reflected waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose, forming fixed nodes and antinodes. For part (b), v=√(T/μ)=√[71.5/(2.03×10⁻³)]=187.7 m s⁻¹. Fixed ends give λ=2L=0.64 m for the first harmonic, so f=v/λ=187.7/0.64=293 Hz, closest to string 2 at 294 Hz. For part (c), both motions have the same frequency and period, but their speeds and wavelengths differ. The string wave is transverse and has position-dependent amplitude, including nodes; sound in air is longitudinal and travels away, transferring energy, while an ideal standing wave has no net energy transfer along the string. In an idealized no-spreading, no-attenuation travelling-wave model, equal-amplitude points are possible, but real emitted sound amplitude generally decreases with distance.
answer.evidence: Pearson Edexcel WPH12_01_2306_MS checked on PDF page 13; visible worked explanation independently recalculated.

parts.given_text: For a string under tension, use v=√(T/μ), where T is the string tension and μ is its mass per unit length.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A loudspeaker at B sends 200 Hz sound toward reflecting sheet A, forming a standing wave. A microphone is moved along AB and its oscilloscope displays the relative amplitude at each position. (i) Explain how a standing wave with nodes and antinodes is formed. (ii) The measured node amplitudes are nonzero and closer to zero nearer A; explain. (iii) Adjacent nodes are 0.84 m apart. Calculate sound speed. (iv) Suggest one uncertainty-reducing method improvement.

answer.text: Official markscheme results: unequal incident/reflected amplitudes explain imperfect nodes; v=336 m s⁻¹; measure multiple node spacings or repeat. Editorial worked explanation: Incident and reflected waves of equal frequency travel oppositely and superpose. In-phase points give antinodes; antiphase points give nodes. Attenuation means the returning wave has smaller amplitude than the incident wave, so destructive interference is incomplete. Close to reflector A the amplitudes are more similar, making minima closer to zero; their difference grows farther away. Adjacent nodes are λ/2, so λ=1.68 m and v=fλ=(200)(1.68)=336 m s⁻¹. Measure across several node intervals and divide, or repeat and average, to reduce fractional uncertainty.
answer.evidence: OCR H156/01 June 2023 markscheme checked across PDF pages 12-13; editorial explanation independently recalculated.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A 1.2 m string vibrates at its second harmonic. The displacement–time graph shown is for a point on the string. What are the wavelength and frequency?

A. 0.6 m; 0.17 kHz
B. 0.6 m; 0.34 kHz
C. 1.2 m; 0.17 kHz
D. 1.2 m; 0.34 kHz

answer.text:
Published key C checked; editorial worked explanation:

C. For a string fixed at both ends, L=nλ/2. At the second harmonic, n=2, so λ=L=1.2 m. The graph completes one cycle from 0 ms to 6.0 ms, giving T=6.0×10⁻³ s and f=1/T=167 Hz=0.17 kHz.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A standing wave is created on a string by two travelling waves. Which statement is not correct?

A. They have the same frequency.
B. They have the same relative phase at every position along the string.
C. They travel in opposite directions.
D. They have the same speed.

answer.text:
Editorial adapted solution (original source key B):

B. The two waves have the same frequency and speed and travel in opposite directions. At any one fixed position their relative phase is constant in time, but it depends on position: for counterpropagating waves the phase difference varies along the string. Therefore they do not have the same relative phase at every position. The original wording, ‘a constant phase relationship’, is ambiguous because it can correctly describe the time-independent phase difference at a fixed position.

evidence.detail: AQA 7408/1 June 2023 published key B, mark-scheme PDF page 26; explanation independently authored and checked.

parts.given_text: Editorial clarification: option B now states that the relative phase is the same at every position. The source’s broader phrase ‘a constant phase relationship’ is preserved in the source record and discussed in the answer.

Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.

original-ib26mb1a-mcq-21:whole.hint: Identify the displacement boundary condition at each end and count the quarter-wavelength sections in the pattern.
notes: An open end is a displacement antinode and a rigid closed end is a displacement node.
An ideal tube with one open and one closed end supports odd harmonics only. The second resonance is the third harmonic, not the second harmonic.

original-ib26mc1a-mcq-21:whole.hint: Use the allowed harmonic numbers for a pipe with unlike boundary conditions, then compare the wavelength ratios.
notes: A displacement node at the closed end and antinode at the open end require an odd number of quarter wavelengths.
Higher harmonics have higher frequency but shorter wavelength in the same medium. The third harmonic wavelength is one third of the fundamental wavelength.

fast-ib-a6e5d76baf5090c2-14:whole.hint: Apply the closed-end node and open-end antinode boundary conditions; the fundamental fits one quarter-wavelength.
notes: A pipe with one closed end supports only odd multiples of its first-harmonic frequency.
With L = λ/4 for the first harmonic, the frequency is V/(4L), and higher allowed modes multiply this by 2n−1.

fast-ib-production-001-a-may-q15:whole.hint: Use the integer-harmonic relation for a string fixed at both ends.
notes: Do not multiply 240 Hz by 5 directly; 240 Hz is already the second harmonic.
The ratio f5/f2 is 5/2, so the fundamental frequency cancels cleanly.

fast-ib-production-001-a-nov-q17:whole.hint: Use the spacing between successive allowed odd harmonics of a closed pipe.
notes: The two given frequencies need not be the first and next numerical integers; closed pipes omit even harmonics.
Successive resonances of a one-end-closed pipe are separated by twice the first-harmonic frequency.

fast-ib-16794b5512ac31d3-3-b:whole.hint: Count the half-wavelength loops in the 120 Hz mode, then scale that integer by the frequency ratio 180/120.
notes: The string length and wave speed are unchanged, so the allowed harmonic frequencies scale with the number of loops.
A correct drawing keeps the same endpoints and adds one loop, giving three equal half-wavelength sections.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-3-b-i.hint: Identify the reflected wave and explain how it combines with the incoming wave inside the pipe.
notes: A standing wave requires superposition of equal-frequency waves travelling in opposite directions.
The closed end supplies the reflection; merely naming resonance does not explain formation of the pattern.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-3-b-ii.hint: Count the quarter-wavelength sections between the closed-end displacement node and open-end displacement antinode.
notes: A closed end is a displacement node and an open end is a displacement antinode.
The displayed mode is not the first harmonic: 1.20 m contains three quarters of a wavelength.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-3-c-i.hint: At P’s horizontal coordinate, compare the solid curve with equilibrium and translate the signed displacement using the arrows.
notes: The vertical plotting direction represents longitudinal displacement; the particle remains inside the horizontal pipe.
Use the solid curve for time t. The dotted curve is the later state and is mainly needed for velocity direction.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-3-c-ii.hint: Compare the solid displacement at time t with the dotted displacement later to determine the direction of change.
notes: Velocity direction follows the change of displacement with time, not the spatial slope of the wave curve.
The velocity arrow lies along the pipe because the air particles oscillate longitudinally.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-3-d.hint: Use the displayed 210 Hz mode to identify the first harmonic, then test whether 140 Hz is an allowed odd multiple.
notes: A pipe with one closed and one open end supports f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁ and other odd multiples only.
At 140 Hz the displacement boundary condition at the open end would be wrong, so resonance is not established.

cross-ed24u5-4:whole.hint: Compare the driving frequency with the system’s natural frequency, then consider the damping.
notes: Resonance is a large forced response when the driving frequency is near a natural frequency. Energy must be supplied by the driver.
More damping reduces the peak response and broadens the resonance. Distinguish driving frequency from the free oscillation that would occur without the driver.

cross-oc24p2-9:whole.hint: Locate the nodes separating the two points before comparing their oscillations.
notes: Points within one loop of a standing wave oscillate in phase; adjacent loops oscillate in antiphase. Amplitude depends on position.
An ideal standing wave forms from opposite-travelling waves of equal frequency and has no net energy transport along the pattern. The nodes remain at zero displacement.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-30:whole.hint: Distinguish a particle’s amplitude from its instantaneous displacement.
notes: Nodes and antinodes describe how amplitude varies with position. An antinode is not a permanently displaced point.

cross-ca25n42-written-5-bi-bii:whole.hint: Heavy damping prevents an overshoot. The given initial velocity also constrains the starting slope.
notes: Do not draw a sinusoid with gradually shrinking amplitude: that represents light damping. Critical damping is the fastest non-oscillatory return; heavy damping is slower.
A displacement–time slope is velocity. Preserve the specified zero initial velocity even though the curve becomes steeper briefly before flattening.

cross-fast-aqa-f44747ff7b639a5d-6-c4:who.hint: Compare each supplied driving frequency with the natural frequency and predict the oscillation amplitude.
notes: Resonance produces a large oscillation amplitude when the driving frequency is close to the system’s natural frequency.
Compare each supplied encounter frequency with 0.13 Hz. Continuing to move puts the driving frequency farther from resonance and reduces heave.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q23:whole.hint: Use adjacent antinode separation to find wavelength, then convert the period into horizontal grid centimetres.
notes: Successive amplitude maxima are adjacent antinodes and are separated by half a wavelength.
A 2.0 ms period occupies four 0.50 ms divisions on the CRO time axis.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q27:whole.hint: Sketch alternating antinodes and nodes, starting and ending with antinodes at the open ends.
notes: For displacement in an open pipe, each open end is an antinode rather than a node.
An open-open mode with three nodes has one more antinode than node.

cross-fast-production-005-a-q25:whole.hint: Use the node–antinode boundary conditions to decide whether all integers or only odd harmonics are allowed.
notes: A closed–open displacement pattern fits one quarter wavelength in the first harmonic.
The allowed frequencies are odd integer multiples of the first harmonic: 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on.

cross-fast-production-005-a-q26:whole.hint: Relate antinode count to harmonic number, then scale that number with frequency.
notes: For a string fixed at both ends, the nth harmonic has n antinodes and n+1 nodes.
Doubling frequency at fixed length and wave speed doubles the number of half-wavelength segments.

cross-fast-edexcel-2decbb656a294fca-18:w.hint: Describe reflection and superposition for formation. For the identification, find wave speed from the supplied law, use λ=2L for two fixed ends, and compare the resulting frequency with the table.
notes: The current guide calls the lowest fixed-string mode the first harmonic; the source’s term ‘fundamental’ refers to the same displayed mode with nodes at both ends.
The source markscheme’s uniform-sound-amplitude comparison is an idealization; geometric spreading and attenuation make real sound amplitude decrease with distance.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-22-stand.hint: For formation, describe superposition of incident and reflected waves and identify fixed constructive and destructive positions. For the speed, convert adjacent-node separation into wavelength first.
notes: A perfect standing wave assumes equal opposite-wave amplitudes; attenuation breaks that condition and leaves residual amplitude at nominal nodes.
Using several node intervals makes the same absolute position uncertainty a smaller fraction of the measured distance.

cross-fast-production-006-a-q14:whole.hint: Use the second-harmonic length relation for wavelength and read one complete period from the time graph.
notes: For the second harmonic of a string fixed at both ends, the string length contains two half-wavelengths, so L=λ.
The time axis is in milliseconds; convert 6.0 ms to 6.0×10⁻³ s before taking its reciprocal.

cross-fast-production-006-a-q15:whole.hint: Distinguish a phase difference that stays fixed in time at one point from a phase difference that is identical everywhere.
notes: A standing pattern requires coherent waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions through the same medium.
This card explicitly clarifies the source’s ambiguous option B; the original paper and published key are preserved in the source record.

cross-fast-production-007-a-a12:whole.hint: Count the half-wavelength sections between fixed-end nodes before using v=fλ.
notes: Nodes at both ends and the centre identify the second harmonic.
